analysis.one_liner: Bans abusive high-cost home-loan practices like balloon payments, prepayment penalties, and financed credit insurance.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan-drafted but single-sponsor Senate bill to curb predatory home lending was referred to the Banking Committee in April 2000, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten federal lending law to stop practices that strip home equity from borrowers with weak credit or low incomes. For high-cost home loans, it would have banned balloon payments, negative amortization (payments that don't even cover interest, so the balance grows), requiring borrowers to pay several months of payments up front, fees financed into the loan, charges to modify or defer a loan, and forced arbitration clauses. Lenders would have had to verify a borrower could repay and ensure the borrower got HUD-approved credit counseling. For all mortgages, it would have banned prepayment penalties, bans on raising the rate after default, and rolling life, disability, or unemployment insurance premiums into the loan. It also set new definitions for points, fees, and broker compensation so these practices couldn't be renamed to dodge the rules, gave the Federal Reserve and FTC enforcement tools, and required buyers of loans to check that the rules were followed.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners taking out high-cost or subprime loans, who are disproportionately elderly, low-income, or living in minority neighborhoods. These borrowers were routinely signed into loans built to fail, losing their homes or years of equity. The bill would have kept more of their equity in their pockets and forced lenders to confirm they could actually afford the payments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High-cost mortgage borrowers, often seniors and low-income homeowners

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits balloon payments, negative amortization, and lumping several payments into the loan proceeds, the structures most commonly used to take a borrower's home through default [S3].
Requires lenders to verify the borrower's debts do not exceed 50 percent of monthly gross income and to provide HUD-approved credit counseling before the loan closes [S3].
Bans prepayment penalties on all residential mortgages, letting borrowers refinance when rates drop instead of paying a fee to leave a bad loan [S3].
Bars financing credit life, disability, and unemployment insurance premiums into a mortgage, a costly add-on that often benefited lenders far more than borrowers [S3].
Forbids lenders from profiting by repeatedly refinancing their own customers into new high-cost loans and from encouraging borrowers to default on existing debts in order to refinance them [S3].
Prohibits forced arbitration clauses in high-cost mortgages, preserving borrowers' right to sue in court [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Subprime and high-cost mortgage lenders, mortgage brokers (whose compensation counts against the points-and-fees limits), and sellers of credit insurance. They would lose the fee streams and loan structures the bill bans. Ordinary borrowers would bear modest indirect costs in the form of counseling requirements and stricter underwriting, and some borrowers with very weak finances could lose access to credit entirely.
analysis.who_pays_short: Subprime lenders, mortgage brokers, and credit insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill requires that a borrower's total monthly debts not exceed 50 percent of gross monthly income, a rigid cutoff that could disqualify some borrowers who could realistically manage a loan, reducing credit access for exactly the people the bill aims to protect [S3].
Mandatory HUD-approved counseling before closing would add a step and delay to every high-cost loan, a real cost to borrowers and lenders even if it prevents bad deals [S3].

Banning all prepayment penalties and financing of fees could push lenders to charge higher upfront rates instead, since lenders need to recover origination costs somehow; the benefits depend on whether competition passes those savings on to borrowers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target practices whose whole point was to strip equity from vulnerable homeowners, and the overwhelming benefit of keeping people in their homes outweighs the costs. The rigid 50 percent debt-to-income test and universal counseling mandate are blunt instruments and could lock out some would-be borrowers, but those are design flaws, not reasons the bill's core purpose was mistaken.

outcome.mechanism: Schumer introduced it in April 2000 and the Banking Committee never acted on it; it sat in committee until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Schumer introduced the Predatory Lending Deterrence Act in the Senate on April 12, 2000 [S5].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which took no further action [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost mortgage lenders, mortgage brokers, and credit insurance sellers kept operating without these restrictions. That mattered: the equity-stripping lending practices this bill targeted continued through the subprime boom of the following decade, until the 2008 financial crisis forced Congress to act.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Banking Committee, where it received no cosponsors and no action.

against.name: Sen. Phil Gramm
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and no other senator cosponsored, so the record shows only that a Democratic sponsor's bill died in a committee chaired by a Republican without any roll-call to measure support.

industries.note: The bill bans the loan structures and fee practices, like balloon payments, negative amortization, financed fees, and repeated refinancing of the same customer, that generated much of the industry's profit from equity-stripping. Lenders would have had to underwrite for ability to repay, cutting off their largest fee source.

All broker compensation would have counted against the points-and-fees cap, and table-funded transactions would be specifically defined so brokers couldn't structure around the rules. This ends the common arrangement where brokers layer hidden fees onto loans.

industries.industry: Credit life, disability, and unemployment insurers
industries.note: The bill bars financing these insurance premiums into mortgages, eliminating the single-premium credit insurance sales that were highly profitable and of little value to most borrowers.

Purchasers of high-cost mortgages would have owed a new due-diligence duty to verify compliance, adding compliance costs, but the bill makes no requirement that they decline to buy compliant loans, so the underlying business continues.
The ban on prepayment penalties applies to all residential mortgages, not just high-cost ones, so mainstream lenders lose a fee option, while facing none of the other high-cost-loan restrictions.
